paras: The killing of Jesse Bishop was the fatal shooting of a Black man by W. T. Russell, a Chattanooga, Tennessee, policeman, in July 1888. Russell was held for murder and then released on $5,000 bail after a habeas corpus hearing. The case drew renewed notice in late August, when the police chief received an anonymous death threat against Russell.

Russell shot and killed Bishop, whom the papers called "a negro," in Chattanooga in mid-to-late July 1888. The only explanation reported was that Bishop was resisting arrest, a claim the Atlanta Constitution's item qualified with "it is alleged." No crime that Bishop was being arrested for is named, and no witness account of the shooting appears in the coverage.

By July 26 a wire brief reported that Russell had been "held for murder" at Chattanooga. On Wednesday, July 25, he was brought before Judge Shepherd on a writ of habeas corpus, and after the examination he was held to bail of $5,000, "which he readily gave." No report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found.

On August 25 Chief of Police Howard received a letter written in red ink and marked with a skull and cross-bones, reading "Death to Russell and all police that shoot a negro." According to the Chattanooga dispatch, the dead man's friends seemed "determined to revenge." No later report of harm to Russell appears in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers and consisted of short wire items. The first brief, which named the victim "Jessie Rogers" and the officer "W. F. Russell," appeared among one-line news paragraphs in the Hillsboro, Ohio, News-Herald, the Big Sandy News, the Hickman Courier, the Macon Beacon and the Ohio Democrat between July 26 and July 28. The bail hearing appeared under "Telegraph Tips" in the Atlanta Constitution and was repeated in Southern news roundups in the Hillsboro Recorder and the Richland Beacon.

The Memphis Appeal ran the Chattanooga threat story under the headline "This is the Way it Begins," stating as fact that Russell had shot Bishop "for resisting arrest." The Richland Beacon carried a condensed version a week later. None of the items gave Bishop's side or any account beyond the officer's.

The July 26 wire brief called the victim "Jessie Rogers," while the bail item and the Chattanooga dispatch both named him Jesse Bishop. The officer's initials also varied between "W. F." in the brief and "W. T." in later reports.

reader.title: Killing of Jesse Bishop
bases: A Chattanooga policeman shot and killed Jesse Bishop, described as a negro, while, by the officer's side's account, Bishop was resisting arrest; no crowd or mob took part (A1, A6, A9).

Three separately worded reports agree that Policeman Russell killed the man at Chattanooga: a July 26 wire brief (A1), a later telegraph item on the habeas corpus hearing (A6), and an Aug. 25 Chattanooga dispatch (A9); the claim that he resisted arrest comes from one side only and is given as 'alleged' in A6.

accounts.label: Wire brief (July 26)
accounts.gist: Policeman W. F. Russell, who shot and killed a negro named Jessie Rogers, was held for murder at Chattanooga.

accounts.label: Telegraph item on the bail hearing
accounts.gist: Russell killed Jesse Bishop a week earlier while, 'it is alleged', Bishop was resisting arrest; on habeas corpus Judge Shepherd held him to $5,000 bail, which he gave.

accounts.label: Chattanooga dispatch (Aug. 25)
accounts.gist: The police chief received a skull-and-cross-bones letter threatening Russell; Russell had shot Bishop five weeks earlier 'for resisting arrest', and the dead man's friends were said to want revenge.

framing.detail: The July killing and bail hearing ran as one-sentence items in wire-news columns ('Telegraph Tips', 'Southern Briefs'), with the resisting-arrest claim marked 'it is alleged' in the bail item.
The Memphis Appeal's Aug. 26 headline 'This is the Way it Begins' put the focus on the threat to the officer and stated that Bishop was shot 'for resisting arrest'.

conflicts.note: The later and more detailed reports, including the Chattanooga-datelined A9, agree on Bishop; 'Rogers' appears only in the one wire brief and its reprints.
Probably a typesetting variant; both name a Chattanooga policeman Russell.

versions.value: Bishop was resisting arrest, 'it is alleged'

conflicts.note: No account other than the officer's side is reported; the earliest brief gives no reason (A1).

record_check.dossier: About mid-to-late July 1888 (a week before a Wednesday, July 25 hearing; five weeks before Aug. 25).
Policeman W. T. Russell of Chattanooga.
Being arrested (resisting arrest, by the officer's side's account); not in custody.
Resisting arrest, reported as 'alleged' in one item and as fact in others.
Russell was held for murder and, after a habeas corpus hearing before Judge Shepherd, released on $5,000 bail.
Ten white-press items in eight papers, July 26 to Sept. 1, 1888.

info: About mid-to-late July 1888: 'a week ago' before a hearing held on Wednesday (July 25) per A6; 'five weeks ago' as of Aug. 25 per A9; the shooting had already happened by the July 26 brief (A1).
Jesse Bishop, a negro (A6, A9, A10); the wire brief names him 'Jessie Rogers' (A1).
No crime is named; the shooting was said to have happened while Bishop was resisting arrest, given as 'alleged' in A6 and as fact in A9 and A10.
Policeman W. T. Russell of Chattanooga (A6, A10); 'W. F. Russell' in the wire brief (A1).
Brought before Judge Shepherd on a writ of habeas corpus on Wednesday (July 25); after the examination he was held to bail of $5,000, which he readily gave.
